label: thm1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm1}
    Let \(0<\beta<1\), and let \(q=q(T) \le T\) be a prime satisfying
    \[\frac{\log q}{\log T} \to \theta,\qquad 0<\theta \le 1.\]
    Then, for every fixed
    \[0<c<\sqrt{2\min\{\theta,1-\beta\}},\]
    we have
    \[\max_{\substack{\chi(\bmod q) \\ \chi \neq\chi_0}}\max_{T^\beta \le t \le T}\Big|L\Big(\frac{1}{2}+\mathrm{i}t,\chi\Big)\Big| \ge \exp\bigg(c\sqrt{\frac{\log T \log_3 T}{\log_2 T}}\bigg)\]
    for all sufficiently large \(T\).

title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md: Since \(q\) is prime and \(\chi\) is non-principal, \(\chi\) is primitive. Therefore, the result follows from \cite[Theorem 5.23]{Iwaniec2004book}.

label: lem2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put \(G(z):= L(1/2+\mathrm{i}t+z,\chi)L(1/2-\mathrm{i}t+z,\overline{\chi})K(-\mathrm{i} z)\). Since \(\chi\) is non-principal, both \(L(s,\chi)\) and \(L(s,\overline{\chi})\) are entire. Hence \(G(z)\) is holomorphic in the strip \(0\leq \Re z\leq a\). Let \(Y>2|t|+2\), and consider the rectangle with vertices \(\pm\mathrm{i} Y\) and \(a\pm\mathrm{i} Y\). By Cauchy's theorem,
\[\Big(\int_{-\mathrm{i} Y}^{a-\mathrm{i} Y}+\int_{a-\mathrm{i} Y}^{a+\mathrm{i} Y}+\int_{a+\mathrm{i} Y}^{\mathrm{i} Y}+\int_{\mathrm{i} Y}^{-\mathrm{i} Y} \Big) G(z)\mathrm{d} z =0.\]

We first show that the integrals over the two horizontal sides tend to zero as \(Y \to \infty\). By Lemma \ref{lem1} and the Phragm\'en--Lindel\"of principle, we have, uniformly for $0\leq \sigma\leq a$,
\[L\Big(\frac12+\sigma+\mathrm{i} v,\chi\Big)\ll_{a,\varepsilon}\big(q(1+|v|)\big)^{1/4+\varepsilon}.\]
Combining this with the growth condition on \(K\), we obtain 
\[\int_{-\mathrm{i} Y}^{a-\mathrm{i} Y}G(z)\mathrm{d} z = o(1) \quad \text{and} \quad \int_{a+\mathrm{i} Y}^{\mathrm{i} Y}G(z)\mathrm{d} z = o(1)\]
as \(Y \to \infty\). Thus, letting \(Y \to \infty\) yields that
\[\int_{-\mathrm{i}\infty}^{\mathrm{i} \infty}G(z)\mathrm{d} z = \int_{a-\mathrm{i}\infty}^{a+\mathrm{i}\infty}G(z)\mathrm{d} z.\]
Writing $z=\mathrm{i} u$ on the left-hand side and $z=a+\mathrm{i} u$ on the
right-hand side, respectively, gives
\begin{align}
\label{lem2-equation}
&\int_\mathbb{R} L\Big(\frac12+\mathrm{i}t+\mathrm{i} u,\chi\Big) L\Big(\frac12-\mathrm{i}t+\mathrm{i} u,\overline{\chi}\Big)K(u)\mathrm{d} u \nonumber\\
&\qquad= \int_\mathbb{R} L\Big(\frac12+a+\mathrm{i}t+\mathrm{i} u,\chi\Big) L\Big(\frac12+a-\mathrm{i}t+\mathrm{i} u,\overline{\chi}\Big) K(u-\mathrm{i} a)\mathrm{d} u.
\end{align}

Since \(a>1/2\), both Dirichlet series on the right-hand side of
\eqref{lem2-equation} converge absolutely, so we may integrate term by term.
Moreover, we have
\[\int_\mathbb{R} K(u-\mathrm{i} a)\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i} u \log k\ell}\mathrm{d} u = (k\ell)^a \widehat{K}(\log k\ell).\]
Substituting this into \eqref{lem2-equation} proves this lemma.

label: lem4
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem4}
    Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be a set of integers with \(|\mathcal{M}| =N\). As \(N \to \infty\), we have
    \[\max_{|\mathcal{M}|=N}\frac{S(\mathcal{M})}{|\mathcal{M}|}=\exp\bigg(\big(2\sqrt{2}+o(1)\big)\sqrt{\frac{\log N\log_3N}{\log_2N}}\bigg).\]
    Moreover, \(\mathcal{M}\) may be chosen so that
\[y_\mathcal{M} := \max_{m\in\mathcal{M}}P^+(m) \ll (\log N)^{6/5},\]
where \(P^+(n)\) denotes the largest prime factor of \(n\).
